```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(transmap)
data(transmap_example)
data_list <- list(Z = transmap_example$z, N = transmap_example$n)
prog <- r_transcca(data_list, K = 2, sumabs = 0.25)
```

transCCA always returns `K` programs, even when there is no variant-gene
association. To decide which programs reflect real coordinated *trans*
effects, compare each program's strength (`d2_score`) with its distribution
under the null.

# 1. Simulating null data

`generate_null_data()` simulates genotypes and expression with no association
between them:

- each variant is drawn as Binomial(2, $f$), with allele frequency $f$
  sampled from the density of the observed minor allele frequencies `maf`
  (restricted to $0.01 < f < 0.5$), then standardized;
- expression is drawn from $N(0, \Sigma_{EE})$, independently of the
  genotypes, so the gene-gene correlation of the real data is kept.

```{r null-data}
set.seed(1)
null_data <- generate_null_data(n = 100, p = 50,
                                maf = runif(1000, 0.05, 0.5),
                                sigma_ee = cor(transmap_example$Y))
str(null_data[[1]])
```

Each replicate is a `data_list` of the form `list(G = , E = )`, so it can be
passed straight to `r_transcca()`. `R > 1` simulates several independent data
sets at once.

# 2. Null distribution of program strengths

`transcca_null()` simulates null data `n_null` times and fits `r_transcca()`
with the same `K` and `sumabs` as the observed analysis. Match the observed
analysis as closely as possible:

- `n`: the sample size of the association statistics;
- `p`: the number of variants in $W$;
- `maf`: the minor allele frequencies of those variants;
- `sigma_ee`: the gene correlation of the expression data;
- `K`, `sumabs` and any `r_transcca()` options (passed through `...`, e.g.
  `normalization`).

```{r null}
set.seed(3)
null <- transcca_null(n_null = 50, n = transmap_example$n,
                      p = nrow(transmap_example$z),
                      maf = runif(1000, 0.05, 0.5),
                      sigma_ee = cor(transmap_example$Y),
                      K = 2, sumabs = 0.25)
dim(null)
round(colMeans(null), 3)
```

Keep `sumabs` fixed. With `sumabs = NULL`, every replicate is re-tuned by
cross-validation, which is slow.

When the observed analysis whitens expression by its in-sample covariance,
use `method = "insample"` so that the null fits are whitened in the same way.

# 3. Empirical p-values

The p-value of program $k$ is the fraction of null replicates whose
`d2_score` for program $k$ exceeds the observed one:

```{r pvalue}
prog$d2_score
transcca_pvalue(prog, null)
```

With `n_null` replicates the smallest attainable non-zero p-value is
$1 / n_\text{null}$, and a p-value of 0 means only that it is below that
bound. Use enough replicates for the significance level of interest (for
example, at least 1,000 for $\alpha = 0.005$).

`transcca_pvalue()` also accepts a numeric vector of observed scores.

# 4. Visualization

`transcca_plot()` compares the observed scores with the null distribution and
marks programs with p-value at or below `alpha`. It returns a summary table
invisibly.

### Bar plot

The null mean of each program is drawn as a bar with $\pm 1.96$ SD error bars,
the observed score as a red triangle and a blue star above significant
programs.

```{r plot-bar, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 4}
tab <- transcca_plot(prog, null, alpha = 0.05)
tab
```

### Box plot

The null distribution of each program is drawn as a box plot, with the
observed score as a red square:

```{r plot-box, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 4}
transcca_plot(prog, null, alpha = 0.05, type = "box")
```

# 5. Keeping significant programs

Pass only significant programs to `transmap_global()`:

```{r keep}
pval <- transcca_pvalue(prog, null)
keep <- names(pval)[pval <= 0.05]
V_sig <- prog$V[, keep, drop = FALSE]
dim(V_sig)
```
